text:
B: Hello! Hello, can you hear me? Oh good, there you are. I'm Danuta.
A: Hi, Danuta. Craig. Yes, I can hear you fine.
B: Lovely. So we have three minutes, no? I never know what to say in three minutes, I talk too much, so you stop me. Have you had your tea yet?
A: Not yet, no. I'll have dinner after this. Probably chicken and rice.
B: Chicken and rice, very good, very healthy. I had a late shift yesterday so today I am off, I made pierogi at the weekend, sixty of them, all in the freezer now. So tonight is easy, just boil.
A: Sixty. That's commitment.
B: My husband says I cook for an army, but then my son comes from Manchester with his little girl and they all disappear, you know? Where are you from, Craig? Your accent, it's not from here, I think.
A: No. Durban originally. South Africa. I've been here about twenty-four years though. I'm in Woodley, near Reading.
B: Oh, South Africa! So far. I am from Poland, near Rzeszów, but I live in Preston now nearly twenty years. So we are both, how do you say, from somewhere else.
A: Ja, that's about right.
B: And what work you do? I guessed from your photo, I think engineer, with the books and the folders.
A: That's right, actually. Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment jobs. Old buildings, checking whether they'll stand up when people knock walls out.
B: Ha, I was right! I'm proud of myself. I work at the hospital, I clean the wards. Eleven years on the same two wards. Everybody knows me, the nurses, the patients. I like it, but my knees, after an early shift, oh.
A: I can imagine. That's a lot of time on your feet.
B: All day walking, mopping. But I like to talk to the old ones, the lonely ones, you know? Some of them nobody visits. Sorry, I talk too much.
A: No, that's fine. Someone's got to.
B: And your family, they are still in South Africa?
A: My parents are, yes. In Durban. My sister's in Australia. I've got a daughter here, she's fifteen. That's her in the photo behind me.
B: She's beautiful. Fifteen, oh, difficult age, no? My daughter at fifteen, I don't want to remember. Now she's in Poland again, I miss her very much.
A: Ja. It's hard, being far from people. I go back to see my folks every eighteen months or so. They're getting on a bit.
B: My mother is eighty-four. I go every summer. Every time I leave I think, maybe last time, you know? It's not easy.
A: No. It's not.
B: But then, phone calls every evening! Video, now, with my granddaughter, she says Polish words to me. So that helps.
A: That's good. My parents aren't great with video calls. Lots of foreheads.
B: Ha! Yes, my mother too, only her ear I see!
A: Do you cook South African food? Sorry, I mean, do you cook much from home? Polish food?
B: All the time! Gołąbki, żurek at Easter, poppy-seed cake at Christmas. And you, you have special food from Durban?
A: I make biltong. Dried meat. I built a drying box in the garage. The latest batch is nearly ready, actually.
B: You built a box for meat! This is very engineer. My Tadeusz would love that, he—
